title: India and Nepal Launch Cross-Border UPI Payments. Millions of Migrant Workers Stand to Benefit.
excerpt: Jaishankar hands over 84 post-earthquake reconstruction projects and launches a digital payment corridor that could reshape how Nepal's workers in India send money home.
body:
India and Nepal have operationalised a cross-border digital payment linkage that connects India's Unified Payments Interface to Nepal's National Payments Interface, a move that could directly benefit an estimated 1.5 million Nepali migrant workers in India who collectively send billions of rupees home every year.

The announcement came on Saturday after External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar held bilateral talks in New Delhi with his visiting Nepali counterpart, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal. The UPI-NPI corridor, built on a memorandum of understanding between India's National Payments Corporation of India and Nepal's NCHL that was signed in June 2023, had taken three years to operationalise. Its launch means that for the first time, a Nepali worker in Mumbai or Delhi can send money home through a phone-based digital transfer rather than relying on slower and more expensive remittance channels.

"Jointly launched the linkage between UPI India and National Payments Interface Nepal for facilitating cross-border personal remittances," Jaishankar confirmed on X after the meeting.

## 84 Projects, One Earthquake's Shadow

The payment corridor was not the only deliverable. Jaishankar also virtually handed over 72 health facilities and 12 cultural heritage projects that India had rebuilt under its post-2015 earthquake reconstruction assistance programme. The 7.8-magnitude earthquake that struck Nepal on 25 April 2015 killed nearly 9,000 people and destroyed thousands of schools, hospitals, and heritage sites. India committed over $250 million to the reconstruction effort.

The handover marks a tangible conclusion to years of bilateral cooperation that has sometimes been overshadowed by political friction between Delhi and Kathmandu. For the Nepali diaspora in India — and for Indian-origin communities with deep familial and cultural ties across the border — the projects represent a rare instance of development diplomacy that has delivered on its promises.

## AI, Language, and a Deeper Digital Stack

Beyond payments and reconstruction, the two ministers witnessed the exchange of a memorandum of understanding between Kathmandu University's Centre for Digital Public Infrastructure and Artificial Intelligence and India's Digital India Bhashini Division. The collaboration will co-create a national digital infrastructure for a "Voice First" language translation platform in Nepal — effectively extending India's multilingual AI stack across the border.

The Bhashini platform, which India has been building as part of its broader digital public goods strategy, currently supports real-time translation across more than a dozen Indian languages. Extending it to Nepal, where dozens of languages are spoken across the country's diverse ethnic landscape, signals a quiet ambition: to make India's digital infrastructure the default backbone for South Asia's digital transformation.

## The Bigger Picture

The bilateral talks covered trade, energy, hydropower development, education, health, digital cooperation, culture, and sports. Both ministers also welcomed the completion of internal processes for the India-Nepal Mutual Legal Assistance Agreement in Criminal Matters, an institutional legal framework to enhance the effectiveness of cross-border criminal investigations and judicial proceedings.

Khanal, who arrived in India on June 5 at Jaishankar's invitation, had flagged the UPI linkage as a priority even before the talks began. "We want to see that happen on the India side too," he told NDTV, referring to enabling digital payments for Nepalis travelling in India.

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with business or familial connections to Nepal, the significance is straightforward. A digital remittance corridor eliminates the friction of hawala networks, reduces transfer costs, and brings cross-border payments into the formal financial system — a shift that both governments have long sought but only now delivered.

The question, as always with India-Nepal relations, is whether the momentum survives the next political cycle in Kathmandu. For now, the deliverables are real: 84 projects handed over, a payment corridor opened, and an AI partnership launched. Whether it amounts to a turning point or a high-water mark will depend on what follows.
